title: Python Sets: A Practical Handbook for 3.11+
summary: A dense, 10-chapter guide covering set foundations, mechanics, performance trade-offs, and practical workflows for Python 3.11+ developers.

chapters.title: 1 Uniqueness and Set Foundations
points: Definition: A set is an unordered collection of unique, hashable elements.
Core Mechanism: Sets use a hash table internally, enabling average O(1) membership testing.
Constraint: Elements must be hashable (immutable types like int, str, tuple); lists and dicts are invalid.
Gotcha: `set()` creates an empty set, while `{}` creates an empty dictionary.
Ordering: Sets do not preserve insertion order; iteration order is arbitrary and implementation-dependent.
Example: `s = {1, 2, 3, 2}` results in `{1, 2, 3}` (duplicates removed).
Comparison: Sets vs Lists: Sets allow O(1) lookup but no indexing; Lists allow O(n) lookup but preserve order.
Hashing: Two objects are equal if `==` is True and `hash()` returns the same value.
Identity: `1` and `True` are considered equal and have the same hash, so they collapse in a set.
Summary: Use sets for membership testing and deduplication, not for ordered sequences.

chapters.title: 2 Creating Sets and Membership
points: Creation: Use literal `{1, 2, 3}` for non-empty sets; use `set()` for empty sets or from iterables.
Conversion: `set(iterable)` is O(n) average; it removes duplicates and loses original order.
Membership: `x in s` is average O(1), worst-case O(n) due to hash collisions.
Example: `s = set('hello')` results in `{'h', 'e', 'l', 'o'}` (duplicates removed).
Gotcha: `set([1, 2, 2, 3])` is `{1, 2, 3}`; the list order is not preserved in the set.
Hashability Check: `hash(x)` must not raise TypeError for `x` to be in a set.
Comparison: `in` on List is O(n); `in` on Set is O(1) average.
Example: `5 in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}` returns `True` instantly regardless of position.
Edge Case: `set()` from a generator consumes it; the generator cannot be reused.
Summary: Prefer sets for frequent membership checks; use lists for ordered data.

chapters.title: 3 Adding and Removing Elements
points: Add: `s.add(x)` adds x if not present; does nothing if present. Returns `None`.
Update: `s.update(iterable)` adds all elements from an iterable. Returns `None`.
Remove: `s.remove(x)` raises `KeyError` if x is not in the set.
Discard: `s.discard(x)` removes x if present; does nothing if absent. No exception.
Pop: `s.pop()` removes and returns an arbitrary element; raises `KeyError` if empty.
Clear: `s.clear()` removes all elements. Returns `None`.
Gotcha: Mutating methods (`add`, `remove`, `discard`, `update`, `clear`) always return `None`.
Comparison: `remove` vs `discard`: Use `remove` for strict validation, `discard` for safe cleanup.
Summary: Choose `remove` for error detection, `discard` for idempotent operations.

chapters.title: 4 Union, Intersection and Differences
points: Union: `s1 | s2` or `s1.union(s2)` returns all elements from both sets.
Intersection: `s1 & s2` or `s1.intersection(s2)` returns elements common to both.
Difference: `s1 - s2` or `s1.difference(s2)` returns elements in s1 but not in s2.
Symmetric Difference: `s1 ^ s2` or `s1.symmetric_difference(s2)` returns elements in either but not both.
Operator Constraint: `|`, `&`, `-`, `^` require both operands to be sets (or frozensets).
Method Flexibility: `.union()`, `.intersection()`, etc., accept any iterable (list, tuple, generator).
Gotcha: `{1, 2} | [2, 3]` raises TypeError; use `{1, 2}.union([2, 3])` instead.
Immutability: These operations return new sets; original sets are unchanged.
Summary: Use operators for set-set ops, methods for set-iterable ops.

chapters.title: 5 Subsets, Supersets and Disjointness
points: Subset: `s1 <= s2` or `s1.issubset(s2)` is True if all elements of s1 are in s2.
Strict Subset: `s1 < s2` or `s1.issubset(s2) and s1 != s2` is True if s1 is a proper subset.
Superset: `s1 >= s2` or `s1.issuperset(s2)` is True if all elements of s2 are in s1.
Strict Superset: `s1 > s2` or `s1.issuperset(s2) and s1 != s2` is True if s1 is a proper superset.
Disjoint: `s1.isdisjoint(s2)` is True if s1 and s2 have no common elements.
Comparison: `<=` allows equality; `<` requires strict containment.
Gotcha: `isdisjoint` is O(min(len(s1), len(s2))) average, not O(1).
Application: Use `issubset` to validate permissions or feature flags.
Summary: Use strict/non-strict operators based on whether equality is allowed.

chapters.title: 6 Set Comprehensions
points: Syntax: `{expr for item in iterable if condition}` creates a new set.
Deduplication: Comprehensions automatically remove duplicates, unlike list comprehensions.
Example: `{x**2 for x in range(5)}` -> `{0, 1, 4, 9, 16}`.
Filtering: `{x for x in data if x > 10}` keeps only elements > 10, unique.
Comparison: List comp `[x for x in data]` preserves order and duplicates; Set comp removes both.
Performance: Set comprehensions are faster than `set(list_comp)` for large iterables.
Gotcha: `{x for x in data}` is a set; `{x: x for x in data}` is a dict.
Example: `data = [1, 2, 2, 3]; {x for x in data}` -> `{1, 2, 3}`.
Use Case: Ideal for extracting unique values from a stream of data.
Summary: Use set comprehensions for unique, unordered transformations.

chapters.title: 7 Frozenset and Hashability
points: Definition: `frozenset` is an immutable, hashable version of a set.
Creation: `fs = frozenset({1, 2, 3})` or `fs = frozenset([1, 2, 3])`.
Hashability: Frozensets can be elements of other sets or keys in dicts.
Example: `s = {frozenset({1, 2}), frozenset({3, 4})}` is valid.
Immutability: `fs.add(4)` raises `AttributeError`; use `fs | {4}` to create a new frozenset.
Comparison: `set` is mutable and unhashable; `frozenset` is immutable and hashable.
Use Case: Representing fixed groups of items (e.g., allowed roles) as dict keys.
Gotcha: `frozenset()` is an empty frozenset; `frozenset({})` is also empty.
Performance: Slightly slower than sets due to immutability checks, but enables hashing.
Summary: Use frozensets when you need a set as a key or element in another set.

chapters.title: 8 Performance and Trade-offs
points: Membership: Set O(1) average vs List O(n) average.
Insertion: Set O(1) average vs List O(1) amortized (but no dedup).
Memory: Sets use more memory per element than lists due to hash table overhead.
Ordering: Sets lose order; lists preserve it. Use `sorted(set)` if order is needed.
Deduplication: Sets deduplicate automatically; lists require manual filtering.
Hash Collisions: Worst-case O(n) for set operations if many elements hash to the same bucket.
Comparison: Use sets for membership, lists for iteration order, dicts for key-value pairs.
Example: `10000 in list_of_10000` is slow; `10000 in set_of_10000` is fast.
Gotcha: `sorted(set)` creates a new list; the set itself remains unordered.
Summary: Choose sets for speed in lookup, lists for order, and accept memory cost.

chapters.title: 9 Practical Validation and Data Workflows
points: Validation: Check if all required fields are present: `required.issubset(data.keys())`.
Deduplication: `unique_users = set(user_list)` removes duplicate user IDs.
Filtering: `valid_ids = all_ids & allowed_ids` finds valid IDs.
Exclusion: `blocked = all_ids - allowed_ids` finds blocked IDs.
Example: `data = {'a': 1, 'b': 2}; required = {'a', 'c'}; required.issubset(data.keys())` -> False.
Workflow: Use sets to track visited nodes in graph traversal (BFS/DFS).
Gotcha: `data.keys()` returns a view; convert to set if needed for set operations.
Application: Use `isdisjoint` to check if two lists have no common elements.
Example: `list1 = [1, 2]; list2 = [3, 4]; set(list1).isdisjoint(list2)` -> True.
Summary: Sets simplify validation, deduplication, and filtering in data pipelines.

chapters.title: 10 Set Cheatsheet and Quick Checks
points: Empty Set: `set()` (not `{}`).
Membership: `x in s` (O(1) avg).
Add: `s.add(x)` (returns None).
Remove: `s.remove(x)` (raises KeyError) vs `s.discard(x)` (no error).
Union: `s1 | s2` (sets only) vs `s1.union(iterable)` (any iterable).
Intersection: `s1 & s2` (sets only) vs `s1.intersection(iterable)` (any iterable).
Difference: `s1 - s2` (sets only) vs `s1.difference(iterable)` (any iterable).
Subset: `s1 <= s2` (non-strict) vs `s1 < s2` (strict).
Frozenset: Immutable, hashable, can be in sets/dicts.
Quick Check: What is `set([1, 2, 2, 3])`? -> `{1, 2, 3}`.
Quick Check: What is `{1, 2} | [2, 3]`? -> TypeError.
Quick Check: What is `s.pop()` on an empty set? -> KeyError.
